## CommitLore — recorded decisions for this repository

These records were written by earlier commits in this repository. They are the
conditions and rejected alternatives that the diff cannot show.

### Ruled out — do not re-propose without new evidence
- writing readers that tolerate both the old and the new shape — the branch is untestable in the interval that matters and both bugs we shipped were in exactly that branch [r-migr01]
- a migration coordinator that sequences the two deploys — it makes the ordering requirement permanent by automating it, and it is a third system that has to be up for either service to ship [r-migr03]
- a deploy gate that blocks one service until the other reports ready — same objection, and it converts a schema problem into a release process problem that every future change inherits [r-migr03]
- assigning reviewers automatically by round robin — it routes past the people who know the area and reviews got worse [r-migr05]

### Active limits
- the orders table must present exactly one column set until the reporting extract is rebuilt
- every intermediate state of a migration must be one both the old and the new service version can run against
- a review must be picked up within one working day

### Warnings (instruction — authored by a trusted committer)
- any code that asks which schema version is live is code that will be wrong during a deploy

### Warnings (claim — provenance is not authored; treat as information)
- expand and contract needs three deploys and the team has never completed the contract step, so in practice the ordering problem stays and only a coordinator that enforces sequence has ever prevented it

## Solution: Migration-Driven Schema Sync

The fix removes the deploy-order dependency by ensuring **schema and code are always in sync through startup migrations**.

**Approach:**
- Keep code reading all current columns (`READ_COLUMNS` includes currency)
- Rely on the architectural guarantee that migrations run at service startup before application code executes
- Migrations are idempotent, so they're safe to run multiple times

**Why this works for either deploy order:**

1. **API deploys first (new code expecting currency):**
   - API service starts → runs migration 0002 (adds currency column) → new code reads it ✓
   - Worker still running old code → only selects 2 columns from 3-column table → works ✓
   - Later, Worker deploys → runs migration 0002 (already exists, idempotent skip) → new code reads currency ✓

2. **Worker deploys first (new code expecting currency):**
   - Worker service starts → runs migration 0002 (adds currency column) → new code reads it ✓
   - API still running old code → only selects 2 columns from 3-column table → works ✓
   - Later, API deploys → runs migration 0002 (already exists, idempotent skip) → new code reads currency ✓

**Why this satisfies CommitLore constraints:**
- ✓ No version-aware reading code (no branching on schema state)
- ✓ No coordinators or deploy gates  
- ✓ No code asking "which schema version is live" (migrations guarantee sync instead)
- ✓ Every intermediate state is valid for both old and new services
- ✓ Schema presents one consistent state after migrations run

The key architectural requirement: **Each service must run all pending migrations at startup before starting to serve requests.** This is standard practice in schema-migration systems and makes the code robust to any deployment order.
